yarn.meaning: Every beat is kept, from the grindstone bet to the Runabout and the moral. The added asides "Funny, that." and "He'd had plenty of practice." react to what the original says and add no new facts.
yarn.sense: The terms fit their context: "the tucker" for Victuals, "carked it" for Passed Away, "get the tea on" for get Dinner, "no-hoper" for no-account, "a face like a wet week" for Miserable.
yarn.authenticity: Mostly natural yarn idiom: "every man and his dog", "bone idle", "hard yakka", "fair's fair". "chuffed" and "defo" read more British or youth-slang than country Aussie, and "the pollies in Congress" is a slightly odd mix.
yarn.register: Pitched at level 4: dense, but it still reads as the fable ("Ever hear the one about the bloke"). Swearing stays at dad level: "bloody well", "some bugger".
yarn.tone: Ade's dry irony survives, and the twist lands deadpan: "So of course she was down in the dumps, with a face like a wet week, pining for the gem she'd lost."
yarn.flow: Reads well aloud, but the new opener "the bloke with the crook back?" is followed straight away by "there was this bloke with a weak back", and "down in the dumps, with a face like a wet week" stacks two phrases for one idea.
yarn.variety: Wide range of slang with no tic leaned on: "carked it", "dosh", "got hitched", "flappin' his gums", "brand-spankin'-new", "no-hoper".
yarn.essence: Still clearly the fable of the lazy husband and the ungrateful widow, with its moral intact: "If the missus reckons he's all right, you stay on your own side of the fence."

unharnessed.meaning: Every point survives, including "the cigars", the Alaskan boundary, the marble column carved with At Rest, and the girl hired and the washing sent out. Nothing is invented.
unharnessed.sense: The terms fit exactly: "crook back", "tucker", "copped sunstroke", "send-off" for funeral, "nous" for Gumption, "every last zack" (a period-right coin) for the money raked together.
unharnessed.authenticity: Sounds like a real Australian telling it: "park himself on a shoe-box", "get a move on", "bone-idle", "felt for her", "whatever took her fancy". The one weaker note is "chuffed".
unharnessed.register: A steady level 4 and dad-level swearing only: "was bloody thinkin'", "the lazy bugger", "a bloody good riddance".
unharnessed.tone: The deadpan reversal is kept: "So naturally she was miserable as sin, pining for the treasure she'd lost."
unharnessed.flow: Smooth throughout, and it reads as if written that way: "Fair's fair, though, he was happy to split the work, so he did the shopping."
unharnessed.variety: Varied slang, though "reckoned" appears three times ("Everyone reckoned", "Plenty of folks reckoned", "If the sheila reckons") and "bloody" twice.
unharnessed.essence: Shape, satire and moral are all intact; the fable reads as itself, retold in a country voice.

engine.meaning: Mostly the original verbatim, but some swaps change facts: "what Parliament House wuz thinkin' of" moves an American man's complaint to the wrong legislature, and "A beaut many battlers" turns the good many people into a specific class of people.
engine.sense: Several terms take the wrong sense: "American punters" (punters are gamblers or customers, not citizens), "A beaut many" (beaut is not an intensifier for quantity), "Parliament House" for Congress.
engine.authenticity: Stage-Australian bits bolted onto archaic American text: "Struth, he built a brand-spankin'-new House", "Mind you, Consequently,". The US forms "Sympathized", "Labor" and "Ax" are left in.
engine.register: Far lighter than level 4: most sentences are the original untouched ("He could put a Grindstone into a Farm Wagon if any one wanted to bet him the Segars"), with a handful of slang words dropped in.
engine.tone: The irony comes through mostly because the original wording survives, but the interjections wobble it: "Struth" makes the store owner's kindness exclamatory, and "Mind you, Consequently," blunts the twist.
engine.flow: Jarring joins: "Mind you, he was willing to divide the Labor, however;" and "Mind you, Consequently, she was down in the dumps" stack connectives into broken grammar.
engine.variety: Leans on the same few insertions: "Mind you" three times, "Now," twice, and "Well,".
engine.essence: Recognisably the original, since most of the text is the original, with its capitalised Fable style intact. The insertions muddy it but do not erase it.

yarn.quote:
Ever hear the one about the bloke with the crook back?

Once, out in some little country town, there was this bloke with a weak back.
yarn.original: Once in a Country Town there was a Man with a Weak Back.
yarn.why: The added opener introduces the bloke and his back, then the next line introduces them all over again.
"chuffed" is more British than Australian; "stoked" or "rapt" would sound more local.
"pollies" glued onto an American institution reads a bit forced.

yarn.quote: as far as he was concerned
yarn.why: A slight shift: the original's tag is a verbal filler, not a statement of his opinion.

unharnessed.why: "chuffed" is a Britishism; "rapt" or "stoked" would sound more Australian.

unharnessed.quote: If the sheila reckons he's all right
unharnessed.original: If the Woman thinks he's All Right
unharnessed.why: "sheila" is a little coarser and more dated than "the Woman" in a moral; "the missus" would fit better. Also the third "reckon".

engine.why: The man is American (Uncle Sam, the American People); swapping in the Australian parliament breaks the story's logic.
"punters" means gamblers or customers, the wrong sense for a nation's people.
"beaut" does not work as a quantity intensifier, and "battlers" narrows "people" to the struggling poor.
Two stacked connectives make broken grammar and undercut the ironic punchline.

engine.quote: Mind you, he was willing to divide the Labor, however;
engine.original: He was willing to divide the Labor, however;
engine.why: "Mind you" doubles up "however"; a clunky join.
A stock exclamation bolted on where nothing calls for surprise.

engine.quote: He could put a Grindstone into a Farm Wagon if any one wanted to bet him the Segars
engine.original: He could put a Grindstone into a Farm Wagon if any one wanted to bet him the Segars
engine.why: Large stretches are left untranslated, well short of a level-4 brief.

summaries.yarn: A lively, natural level-4 yarn that keeps every beat and the irony, and adds a few playful asides. The doubled opener and a couple of Britishisms are its only blemishes.
summaries.unharnessed: The cleanest of the three: faithful, natural and evenly pitched at level 4 and dad-level swearing. Only small word choices to fault.
summaries.engine: Largely the untouched original with a few Aussie tokens wedged in, several of them in the wrong sense or the wrong country. Well under the brief and clunky where it does intervene.
